steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on crosslingual story generation with large language models, where a story plan in English is used to prompt the model to write a story in another language. Cover background on story generation and planning, the new task, the plan types we compare, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Background: early story generation systems
- Pretrained language models and planning for story generation
- New task: crosslingual story generation from English plans
- Approach: prompting large pretrained language models
- Plan representations and new dataset
- Findings and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background: early story generation systems
  - fascination since early days of AI
  - substantial knowledge engineering; symbolic domain models of legal characters and actions
  - relied on symbolic planning and case-based reasoning
- Pretrained language models and planning
  - large pre-trained language models (PLMs): common framework, no manual knowledge engineering
  - fluent, naturalistic text, but struggle with coherence (logical progression of events), repetitive
  - fix: decompose into planning an outline/sketch, then elaborating (descriptions, specific details)
  - plan forms so far: keywords (events, phrases); sequence of actions; plus characters and setting; control tokens
- New task
  - planning for story generation shown only monolingually, mostly English
  - question: does planning help across languages?
  - task: given English plan, generate coherent narrative in target language consistent with plan
  - challenges: plans give only basic plot info; model must flesh out plot + fluent target-language text while staying true to plan; storytelling traditions differ across cultures/languages
- Approach
  - creative and reasoning capabilities of pretrained LMs; strong on many tasks and languages
  - unified framework: one PLM for any target language, no further modification
  - hand-designed prompts ("prompting" / "in-context learning"): free-form instruction + few examples; here plans and their stories
- Plan representations and dataset
  - inspired by discourse structure theories and narrative fiction
  - content: list of entities; sequence of actions; events around the three-act structure (setup, conflict, resolution)
  - form: keywords, prosaic text, question-answer pairs
  - new dataset: stories in 31 linguistically diverse languages, from the Global African Storybook Project
- Findings and contributions
  - three-act structure -> better stories across languages than less detailed plans
  - hypothesis: inner structure; questions point to important events (setup, plot, resolution), improve coherence
  - LLMs generate fluent narratives in many languages despite mostly English pretraining
  - contributions: (a) new task + dataset; (b) study of plans and prompt formulations; (c) automatic + human evaluation: three-act QA plans more controllable, more coherent

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Automated story generation has fascinated people since the early days of artificial intelligence. The first story generation systems needed a lot of knowledge engineering to create symbolic domain models describing legal characters and their actions, and almost all of them relied on symbolic planning and case-based reasoning.

Large pre-trained language models (PLMs) have given AI story generation a common framework and there is no need for manual knowledge engineering anymore. They can produce relatively fluent and naturalistic text, but language models have trouble maintaining story coherence, that is the logical progression of events, and they can also be repetitive. To make stories more coherent and to control the trajectory of events, attempts often split the generation task into planning an outline or sketch and then elaborating on it, for example by filling in descriptions and specific details of each story. In previous work story plans have been represented by keywords such as events or phrases, by a sequence of actions, sometimes combined with information on characters and setting, and by control tokens.

Previous work has shown that planning is effective for story generation, but only in a monolingual setting, mostly English. We look at whether planning also helps automatic story generation across languages. We introduce a new task, crosslingual story generation: given a plan in English, the model has to generate a coherent narrative in a target language that is consistent with what the plan contains. This task is hard for several reasons. First, the plans only give basic plot information about the story. The model has to flesh out these plot elements and generate fluent text in the target language, and it has to stay true to the original plan at the same time. Also, story telling traditions are different between cultures and languages, and good stories for human readers would need to observe this.

- approach: use creative/reasoning capabilities of pretrained LMs (strong on many tasks and languages); one PLM for any target language, no modification; prompting / in-context learning: free-form instruction + few examples (plans + their stories)
- plan representations: inspired by discourse structure theories and narrative fiction; content = list of entities, sequence of actions, events around three-act structure (setup, conflict, resolution); form = keywords, prosaic text, question-answer pairs
- dataset: stories in 31 linguistically diverse languages from the Global African Storybook Project
- findings: three-act structure gives better stories across languages; questions inform model of important events -> coherence; LLMs fluent in many languages despite mostly English pretraining
- contributions (a) task + dataset (b) study of plans/prompts (c) automatic + human results: three-act QA plans more controllable and coherent

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Automated story generation has fascinated people since the early days of artificial intelligence. The first story generation systems needed a lot of knowledge engineering to create symbolic domain models describing legal characters and their actions, and almost all of them relied on symbolic planning and case-based reasoning.

Large pre-trained language models (PLMs) have given AI story generation a common framework and there is no need for manual knowledge engineering anymore. They can produce relatively fluent and naturalistic text, but language models have trouble maintaining story coherence, that is the logical progression of events, and they can also be repetitive. To make stories more coherent and to control the trajectory of events, attempts often split the generation task into planning an outline or sketch and then elaborating on it, for example by filling in descriptions and specific details of each story. In previous work story plans have been represented by keywords such as events or phrases, by a sequence of actions, sometimes combined with information on characters and setting, and by control tokens.

Previous work has shown that planning is effective for story generation, but only in a monolingual setting, mostly English. We look at whether planning also helps automatic story generation across languages. We introduce a new task, crosslingual story generation: given a plan in English, the model has to generate a coherent narrative in a target language that is consistent with what the plan contains. This task is hard for several reasons. First, the plans only give basic plot information about the story. The model has to flesh out these plot elements and generate fluent text in the target language, and it has to stay true to the original plan at the same time. Also, story telling traditions are different between cultures and languages, and good stories for human readers would need to observe this.

We generate stories in several languages using the creative and reasoning capabilities of pretrained language models, which recently got strong performance on various tasks and in many languages. PLMs give us a unified modeling framework for the task. We do not build a different model for each language; the PLM is used to generate stories in any target language without further modification. Following previous work, we use a class of hand-designed prompts that is called "prompting" or "in-context learning". The prompt starts with a free form instruction, and after that there are a small number of examples showing how the task is solved. For us, the prompts contain plans and the stories that go with them.

We also investigate which plans are best for crosslingual story generation. We take inspiration from theories of discourse structure and narrative fiction and create plan representations that differ in form and in content. For content, we formulate plans as a list of entities, as a sequence of actions, and as events around the three-act structure, which is a popular story writing technique that divides a narrative into three parts: the setup, the conflict, and the resolution. For form, plans are keywords, prosaic text, and question-answer pairs. To help research in this area we also create a new dataset with stories in 31 linguistically diverse languages, collated from the Global African Storybook Project.

Our results show that the three-act structure gives better stories (across languages) than less detailed alternatives. We think this is because of the inner structure of the plan: the questions tell the model about the important events (setup, plot, and resolution) and this improves the coherence of the story. Our work also shows that large language models can generate fluent narratives in multiple languages even though they are mostly pretrained on English data. Our contributions are: (a) we propose a new task of crosslingual story generation with planning and present a new dataset for it; (b) we do a comprehensive study of different plans and prompt formulations for crosslingual story generation; and (c) we present results, from automatic and human assessments, which confirm that plans following the three-act structure expressed as question-answer pairs are more controllable and generate more coherent narratives.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Automated story generation has met with fascination since the early days of artificial intelligence. Early story generation systems required substantial knowledge engineering to create symbolic domain models describing legal characters and their actions, and almost ubiquitously relied on symbolic planning [1,2,3,4,5,6] and case-based reasoning [7,8,9].

The advent of large pre-trained language models (PLMs; [10,11,12,13]) has provided a common framework for AI story generation, removing the need for manual knowledge engineering. Despite their ability to produce relatively fluent and naturalistic text, language models struggle to maintain story coherence — the logical progression of events — and may also become repetitive. Attempts to improve the coherence of stories and control the trajectory of events often decompose the generation task into planning an outline or sketch and then elaborating on it, e.g., by filling in descriptions and specific details of each story. Story plans have previously been represented by keywords such as events or phrases [14,15,16], a sequence of actions [17,18], optionally combined with information on characters and setting [19], and control tokens [20,21,22,23].

Previous work has demonstrated the effectiveness of planning for story generation only in a monolingual setting, focusing mainly on English [24,25]. We consider whether planning brings advantages to automatic story generation across languages. Specifically, we introduce a new task of crosslingual story generation: given a plan in English, generate a coherent narrative in a target language that is consistent with the contents of the plan. The task is challenging for several reasons. First, the plans only provide basic plot information about the story. The model needs to flesh out these plot elements and generate fluent text in the target language while staying true to the original plan. Moreover, story telling traditions differ amongst cultures and languages [26], and felicitous stories meant for human readers would need to observe them.

We generate stories in several languages by leveraging the creative and reasoning capabilities of pretrained language models [13,27], which have recently achieved strong performance on various tasks and in many languages [28,29,30]. PLMs provide a unified modeling framework for our task. Rather than building a different model for each language, the PLM is used to generate stories in any target language without further modification. Following [12], we consider a class of hand-designed prompts referred to as "prompting" or "in-context learning". The prompt starts with a free form instruction, followed by a small number of instances showing how the task is solved. In our case, prompts contain plans and their corresponding stories.

We further investigate which plans are best suited for crosslingual story generation. Drawing inspiration from theories of discourse structure [31,32,33] and narrative fiction [34], we create plan representations that differ in form and content. In terms of content, we formulate plans as a list of entities, a sequence of actions, and events revolving around the three-act structure [35], a popular story writing technique that divides a narrative into three distinct parts: the setup, the conflict, and the resolution. In terms of form, plans are keywords, prosaic text, and question-answer pairs. To facilitate research in this area, we also create a new dataset containing stories in 31 linguistically diverse languages collated from the Global African Storybook Project.

Our results show that the three-act structure leads to better stories (across languages) compared to less detailed alternatives. We hypothesize this is due to the inner structure of the plan, i.e., the questions inform the model of important events (setup, plot, and resolution) and improve the coherence of the story. In addition, our work shows that large language models are capable of generating fluent narratives in multiple languages while being pretrained mostly on English data. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: (a) we propose a new task of crosslingual story generation with planning and present a new dataset for it; (b) we conduct a comprehensive study of different plans and prompt formulations for crosslingual story generation; and (c) we present results, based on automatic and human assessments, which confirm that plans following the three-act structure expressed as question-answer pairs are more controllable and generate more coherent narratives.
